title: One detector per cause
choice: Five detectors run independently over the whole file, and each reports its own intervals. A storm and a jammer inside it come back as two overlapping detections.
rejected: One classifier that gives each moment a single cause, as the baseline does. It cannot report TRN-05 or TRN-08, which sit inside a storm.
Splitting a storm around the event inside it. The scorer matches one detection to one label, so a split storm becomes one match plus extra false positives.
evidence: Three of the 12 dev episodes overlap another one: TRN-05 and TRN-08 sit inside the TRN-02 storm, and TRN-06 sits inside TRN-09 on the same tractor. The baseline misses TRN-05 and TRN-08 and leaves two fragments behind as false positives.
limitation: Independent detectors can read one event two ways. A single machine losing signal is the open case: it is reported as a fault, and a jammer beside one tractor would look the same. A second receiver on the machine would separate them.

title: Telemetry sets the clock, and only working tractors count
choice: Start and end times come from the 1 Hz telemetry, and every rule ignores the seconds when a tractor is parked.
rejected: Timing from the sky feeds. Kp arrives every 3 hours and S4 every 15 minutes, which is too coarse for the 5-minute onset window.
Counting parked tractors. The baseline does, and it starts TRN-01 75 minutes early.
evidence: TRN-01's label starts at 11:00:00, the second the tractors start moving. The sag began at 09:45 while they were parked. With the working mask the detector starts at 11:00:00. The baseline starts at 09:45 and earns no onset credit for that episode.
limitation: Working is decided by speed above 1 m/s. A tractor that stopped briefly mid-field during an episode would split it. A work-state signal from the implement would be firmer than speed.

title: A model of how much loss the sky explains
choice: The signal loss the sky explains is 2.1 + 18 × S4 dB once S4 reaches 0.31, and zero below that. Every other rule measures against it.
rejected: Kp as the storm test. Kp is planet-wide and arrives every 3 hours. On May 5 it read 5.7 from 06:00, while the farm's signal was normal until 09:45 apart from one 15-minute dip.
Step detection on telemetry alone. A storm changes strength mid-episode (8 dB to 14 dB at 10:00 on May 5), and without S4 that step looks like a new event.
evidence: Fitted to the May 5 storm: 7.8 dB at S4 0.317, 9.6 at 0.418, 13.8 at 0.648, and 16.4 at 0.795, with residuals under 0.1 dB. Those values are measured against a normal level of 45.0 dB-Hz. The detector's own normal is a median over all three days, 44.8 dB-Hz, so inside the code the prediction runs about 0.2 dB above the measured drop. S4 between 0.27 and 0.30 produced no sag. In the sensitivity sweep, moving the slope or the threshold by 25% changes nothing on dev.
limitation: It rests on one storm day in one simulator. If S4 lagged the farm by one 15-minute sample, the start of a storm would look unexplained. A second storm, or S4 at a 1-minute cadence, would test both.

title: Jamming is the loss the sky does not explain
choice: Jamming is reported where some working tractor has 6 dB or more of loss beyond the S4 prediction. Tractors whose median unexplained loss is 4.5 dB or more are listed, and two or more make it jamming.
rejected: Unequal loss across tractors as the jamming test. TRN-05 is jamming, and every tractor loses the same 12 dB.
Kp below 5 as a condition, as in the baseline. It misses any jammer that operates during a storm.
evidence: TRN-03 leaves 16.5, 14.0, and 19.3 dB unexplained with S4 at 0.05. TRN-05 leaves 12.1, 11.9, and 12.0 dB on top of a 10 dB storm sag. In TRN-04, T1 at 5.5 dB and T3 at 8.0 dB are in the label and T2 at 2.8 dB is not, so the cut sits between 2.8 and 5.5.
limitation: TRN-04 pins both thresholds. Raising the trigger to 7.5 dB splits it into pieces, and raising the cut to 5.6 dB loses it. A jammer weaker than TRN-04 is missed. Per-satellite C/N0 would show a jammer's direction and allow a lower threshold.

title: Kp is context, never a test
choice: Kp never decides a class or a start time. It adds 0.05 to space weather confidence when it reaches 5, and the evidence quotes it as global context.
rejected: Kp as a gate, as in the baseline: at or above 5 for space weather, below 5 for jamming.
evidence: On May 5, Kp fell from 9.0 to 3.0 at 15:00 while the storm at the farm ran until 16:00, and from 6.8 to 3.0 at 21:00 while it ran until 22:00. The baseline relabels both final hours as jamming, which accounts for two of its five false positives.
limitation: Ignoring Kp gives up early warning. Kp rose at 06:00 on May 5, hours before the main impact at the farm. A forecast product would be the right use for it.

title: An interference report supports jamming, and a missing one says nothing
choice: A report that arrives within 45 minutes after the start, with the farm inside its semi-major radius, adds 0.15 to jamming confidence, or 0.05 if the report's own confidence is under 0.5. A missing report subtracts nothing. Reports never set a start time.
rejected: Requiring a report before calling jamming. TRN-05 has none.
Using the report time as the start. Reports arrive 10 to 30 minutes late.
evidence: RFI-001 arrived 14.8 minutes after TRN-03 began, 0.71 km from the farm. RFI-002 arrived 10.7 minutes after TRN-04, 1.04 km away. TRN-05 has no report. RFI-004 (confidence 0.35, issued while the tractors were parked, 4.8 km away) matches no detection.
limitation: The reports give an ellipse without an orientation, so the test uses the semi-major length and can accept a report whose ellipse points away from the farm. An orientation or a bearing would fix that.

title: Spoofing is a drift on one tractor with a healthy signal
choice: Spoofing is one tractor whose smoothed cross-track error is 1 m or more above the other working tractors while its unexplained signal loss stays under 3 dB. The start is walked back by the time the drift took to double.
rejected: A fixed cross-track limit. In a storm every tractor spikes past 1 m.
Requiring normal signal strength, as the baseline does. It misses TRN-08, where a storm has lowered the signal on every machine.
The threshold crossing as the start. It comes 4 to 11 minutes after the label's start.
evidence: The starts found are 3 s, 1 s, and 170 s from the labels for TRN-06, TRN-07, and TRN-08. The drifts climb at 0.14, 0.24, and 0.12 m per minute. In TRN-03, T1 also wanders, but its unexplained loss is 16.5 dB, so it is not called spoofing.
limitation: The walk-back assumes a steady drift. A spoofer that jumps the position, or drifts and pauses, would get a late start. Cross-track error here comes from an idealized monitor. A real receiver would need wheel odometry or an IMU to see the drift at all.

title: Faults show in dropout rate and link flaps, not in average signal
choice: An antenna fault is one tractor whose weakest satellite sits 12 dB or more below its mean signal for at least 12% of a 10-minute window. A link fault is the correction link dropping in bursts less than 5 minutes apart for at least 5 minutes.
rejected: Mean signal strength as the fault signal. In TRN-09 the mean holds at 44.8 dB-Hz.
Link down for three minutes straight, as in the baseline. In TRN-10 the longest burst is 16 seconds.
evidence: In TRN-09, T2 has dropouts 24% of the time against 3% on the other tractors. In TRN-10, T1's link is down 30% of the time while its signal stays at 45.0 dB-Hz. The starts found are 90 s early and 1 s late.
limitation: Lowering the dropout gap to 9 dB counts storm and jamming noise as dropouts and produces ten false faults on dev. Per-satellite C/N0 would show whether one satellite or one side of the antenna is failing.

title: Multipath is a dip that recurs at one place, reported on every pass
choice: Multipath is a 10 to 40 second dip of the weakest satellite, 9 dB or more below the mean, at the latitude where a tractor's dips keep recurring. Every pass is reported as its own short detection.
rejected: Reporting one representative dip. Only one pass is scored, and dev gives no way to tell which.
Reporting dips anywhere in the field. On the two dev days about 555 short dips fall away from the headland.
evidence: On the two dev days each tractor dips at latitude 46.907 about 324 times, once every 356 seconds while working. Both dev labels are found, one to the second and one a second early. The dips elsewhere in the field are not reported.
limitation: The submission carries about 486 multipath reports, close to the validator's limit of 500. Location uses the reported latitude, which is displaced during spoofing. A site survey naming the obstruction would replace the inference.

title: Confidence and evidence come from the same numbers
choice: Each detector records what it measured. Confidence is 0.60 plus or minus fixed weights for those facts, kept between 0.05 and 0.95, and the four evidence sentences are written from the same numbers.
rejected: One confidence value for every detection. The baseline uses 0.5.
A statistical model of confidence. Twelve episodes cannot fit one or check one.
evidence: Dev confidences run from 0.50 for TRN-05 (equal loss inside a storm, no report) to 0.95 for TRN-03 (graded loss, a report, a quiet sky). Because both outputs read one set of facts, the text cannot contradict the number.
limitation: The weights are judgment. Whether 0.8 means right 80% of the time is unknown. More labeled episodes would allow a calibration check.

title: One machine losing signal is reported as a fault
choice: If only one working tractor has unexplained signal loss, it is reported as an equipment fault with confidence capped at 0.45, and the evidence names a nearby jammer as the alternative.
rejected: Calling it jamming. One machine cannot show the footprint across machines that a transmitter leaves.
Reporting nothing. A machine with 6 dB or more of unexplained loss should be looked at.
evidence: Dev has no such case, so this rule rests on reasoning. Both readings lead to stopping that one machine.
limitation: It is untested on labeled data. A jammer that reaches only one tractor on evaluation day will be reported as a fault. Per-satellite C/N0 or a second antenna would separate the two.

title: Thresholds are frozen on dev, and evaluation is run once
choice: Every threshold was set on the two dev days. The configuration is frozen in a commit before the evaluation output is looked at, and nothing learned from that output changes it.
rejected: Adjusting thresholds after looking at evaluation detections. With no labels there, any adjustment is a guess that happens to look good.
evidence: The dev score is 40.00 of 40 against the baseline's 20.15, which is expected because the thresholds were chosen there. The sensitivity sweep moves each threshold by 25%, and 17 of 20 moves change nothing.
limitation: A full dev score says nothing about evaluation day. The sweep and the stated limits are the measure of how far the result can be trusted.
